turns.t: Thanks for seeing us. Darragh has had a cold since Sunday and last night I heard a whistling in his chest.
You were right to bring him. Hello Darragh. Good boy, sit on Mammy's knee. How old is he? ~
He's two and a half. ~
Tell me about the whistling. Is it there all the time?
It's mostly when he breathes out. It comes and goes. It was loudest at about two this morning.
Mammy, nose. ~
His nose is running, love. ~
Is he feeding and drinking normally? ~
Yes, he's grand in himself. He's still playing, he ate his breakfast, and he's been drinking his milk. ~
And any temperature? Has he felt hot at all?
No, I checked him this morning, he's not hot. No temperature at all.
That's what I wanted to hear. Let me listen to his chest. Darragh, can I put my stethoscope on your tummy? ~
Cold! ~
It's cold, isn't it? I'll warm it up for you. Breathe in and out like a doggy.
Is he wheezing? ~
There's a bit of wheeze on both sides when he breathes out, but the air's moving well, there's no work of breathing and no sucking in under the ribs.
Oh, that's good. ~
I'd say this is a viral wheeze, brought on by his cold, which is very common in toddlers.
Will he grow out of it? ~
Most children do. It tends to be triggered by colds and fade as they get bigger. ~
Does he need anything for it? I've got a nebuliser at home from my niece. ~
Not today. He doesn't need anything, and I wouldn't use someone else's equipment. We'll see how he gets on. ~
Okay. And what should I do? ~
Keep him drinking, let him rest, and keep the room smoke-free. Raise his head a little at night if he'll tolerate a pillow.
He hates pillows. ~
Then don't worry about that one. ~
And when would I be worried? ~
If he's breathing fast, you can see his tummy sucking in, he can't finish a sentence or a feed, or his lips go a bit blue, call 999.
Oh God. Okay. ~
I don't expect it, but I'd rather you know. And if the wheeze is still there after five days, or he's not feeding, bring him back.
Five days, got it. ~
Well done, Darragh. You were great. ~
Bye bye! ~
